title: Tzav: the thanks offering (Leviticus 7:12)
hook: after a rescue, a thanks offering; midrash says thanks alone will never cease

segments.voice: Yesterday, the priest's first job: lifting yesterday's ashes. Your line was clear the ashes first. What did you clear? Day three hundred eighty-seven.

Spend an hour in an Israeli supermarket, a taxi or a café, and today's word comes at you again and again. Todah. It's how you say thank you in Hebrew. Todah for the change, todah for the coffee, todah rabbah, thanks a lot. But before it was the word for thanks at a checkout counter, it was the name of an offering. A very particular one, brought by a very particular kind of person: someone who had just been rescued.
screen: `TODAH: THANK YOU.` → `AT THE CHECKOUT, IN THE TAXI.` → `FIRST, AN OFFERING.`

segments.voice: Leviticus lists a family of offerings called peace offerings, and the first kind is this one. In the JPS 1917 translation: "If he offer it for a thanksgiving." Who brings it? Rashi, drawing on the Talmud's reading of Psalm one hundred seven, names four kinds of people who come through danger. Those who cross the sea. Those who cross the desert. Those who recover from serious illness. Those set free from prison. Each has been rescued, and the todah is how they say so. The offering came with a lot of bread, forty loaves by the rabbis' count, and the Torah says it all had to be eaten the same day and night. Some commentators point out the result: you couldn't eat forty loaves alone. You had to invite people in, and over the meal, you'd tell them what happened to you. The thanks became a party, and the party became a story. And then a midrash, in Leviticus Rabbah. It says that in the time to come, all the offerings will cease, except the thanks offering. All the prayers will cease, except the prayer of thanks. The idea seems to be that when everything is mended, no one will need to ask for anything, or atone for anything, but people will still say thank you. Today, with no Temple, the custom lives on in a blessing called ha-gomel, said in synagogue by someone who has come through danger, with the congregation answering. In this teaching, thanks is the one offering with no end date.
screen: `IF HE OFFER IT FOR A THANKSGIVING.` · `FOUR WHO ARE RESCUED.` · `FORTY LOAVES: INVITE PEOPLE IN.` · `ONLY THANKS WILL NEVER CEASE.` · then, large: `THANKS OUTLASTS EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give thanks for a rescue. Settle, and breathe. Think of a time you came through something: a scary diagnosis that turned out fine, a near miss on the road, a hard year you survived, a moment someone pulled you out. Let yourself remember it clearly, without rushing. Who helped? What could have happened, and didn't? If you pray, you can say todah to God. If not, say it to the people who were there, even just in your mind. The bell holds the time.
Todah. Thanks. The offering brought after a rescue, and still the everyday Hebrew word for thank you.
Your line: thanks outlasts everything. Today, tell one person the story of a rescue, and thank someone who was part of it. Day three hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: A person who has come through danger, such as serious illness, a dangerous journey or release from captivity, recites the blessing ha-gomel at the Torah reading, and the congregation responds.

fork.setup: you've just recovered from a serious illness. you bring a thanks offering, with forty loaves, and it all has to be eaten by morning. what do you do?
options: eat what you can and throw out the rest.
invite friends and tell them what happened.
give the bread back to the priests.
fork.reveal: commentators point out that you'd have to invite people in. the thanks becomes a meal, and the meal becomes the story of your rescue.

original.note: Hebrew: thanks, and the name of the thanks offering in Leviticus 7:12.

trapdoor: what you thought: todah means thank you.
what it means: it first named an offering brought by the rescued, shared over a meal with many people.
what a scholar hears: Berakhot 54b derives the four who must give thanks from Psalm 107; Leviticus Rabbah 9:7 says the todah alone will never cease.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): cut unsourced 'dozens of times', 'one of the first words any visitor learns' and 'every Israeli'; the four rescued are now Rashi on 7:12 drawing on the Talmud and Psalm 107 (Berakhot 54b is about giving thanks, not the offering itself); the 'line from the hook' slip fixed; the end-time explanation framed as an interpretation; ending no longer repeats day 381's 'the altar is gone'.
Leviticus 7:12 quoted from JPS 1917; confirm wording.
Berakhot 54b (four who must give thanks, from Psalm 107) and Menachot 77b (forty loaves: ten each of four kinds): confirm.
The 'invite people in and tell the story' reading is attributed to commentators generally (e.g., Netziv, Abarbanel); confirm or name.
Leviticus Rabbah 9:7 (all offerings cease except the todah; all prayers except thanksgiving): confirm.
Birkat ha-gomel is said at the Torah reading in the presence of a minyan; confirm wording.
